To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CBT does _not_ transfer learning from non-overlapping domains, and the reason is that CBT is based on a flawed assumption.

(1) the CBT technique proposed by Li et al. does not work in the absence of overlapping data, (2) the CBT results reported by Li et al are due to an implementation mistake, and (3) the proposed technique is unable to transfer knowledge in the absence of shared characteristics between the source and target domains.

(1) CBT is not a cross-domain recommender technique, as the authors claim, because it does not transfer knowledge between nonoverlapping domains; (2) CBT is an item-item recommender technique that is not able to exploit the knowledge contained in the user-item matrix; (3) CBT is a co-clustering technique with the same characteristics of any other co-clustering technique, i.e. its accuracy in recommending items is not better than the accuracy of a simple item

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CBT is not a cross-domain technique.
cross-domain recommender systems are not able to transfer knowledge without overlap.
CBT is a cross-domain recommender technique that requires overlapping domains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CBT does transfer knowledge only when source and target data overlap.
, in the absence of overlapping users or items, CBT is not able to transfer knowledge and thus it is not effective.
CBT does transfer knowledge between non overlapping domains, but only if the source and target domains are linked by a common third domain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cross-domain CF techniques that do not rely on overlapping data are not able to transfer knowledge from source to target domain.
cross-domain recommendations without overlapping domains cannot work.
CBT is not a viable technique for cross-domain recommendations.
